description: Western art from the caves to Conceptual art, plus how to look at a painting, materials and techniques, and anchors for Chinese, Japanese and Islamic traditions. Focus: recognising a style, what it reacted against, and what technique enabled it.

notes.front: What is the focal point of a picture, and how do painters create one?
notes.back: Where the eye lands first. Made by the strongest light–dark contrast, converging lines, a face or gaze, saturated colour, or an off-centre 'strong point'.
notes.analogy: The hero element on a landing page: everything else is laid out to lead you to it.

notes.front: Rule of thirds vs golden section: what do both achieve?
notes.back: Both move the subject off centre so the picture isn't static. Thirds: a 3×3 grid; golden section: a 0.618 split. In practice the lines nearly coincide.

notes.front: Why did Renaissance painters favour a pyramidal composition?
notes.back: Broad base, apex at the main head: stable, calm, and it leads the eye upward to the key figure (Leonardo's Madonnas, Raphael).
notes.extra: Contrast: Baroque painters deliberately broke the pyramid with diagonals to add motion.

notes.front: Horizontal/vertical vs diagonal composition: emotional effect?
notes.back: Horizontals and verticals read as calm, stable, monumental (Classical, Renaissance). Diagonals read as movement and drama (Baroque, Romanticism).
notes.analogy: A standing column vs a falling tree: the same line, tilted, becomes an event.

notes.text: Colour has three dimensions: {{c1::hue}} (where on the wheel), {{c2::value}} (light vs dark) and {{c3::saturation}} (intense vs greyed).

notes.front: What are complementary colours, and why place them side by side?
notes.back: Opposites on the wheel: red/green, blue/orange, yellow/violet. Adjacent, each looks more intense; mixed, they cancel to grey-brown.
notes.extra: Example: Van Gogh's Night Café (red walls, green ceiling) and Monet's orange sun on blue water.

notes.front: Warm vs cool colours: how do they shape space in a picture?
notes.back: Warm (red, orange, yellow) seem to advance; cool (blue, green, violet) recede. Painters push distance back with blue and pull foregrounds forward with warmth.

notes.front: What is value, and why do teachers say it matters more than hue?
notes.back: The light–dark scale. Value carries form, depth and legibility: a painting that reads in greyscale works. Hue is mostly mood.
notes.extra: Test: squint, or look at a black-and-white photo of the painting. If the composition collapses, the values are wrong.

notes.front: What is chiaroscuro?
notes.back: Modelling form through strong gradations of light and shadow so figures look solid and three-dimensional (Leonardo, Caravaggio, Rembrandt).

notes.front: Chiaroscuro vs tenebrism: how to tell?
notes.back: Chiaroscuro: gradual light–dark modelling for volume. Tenebrism: a violent spotlight with most of the canvas in black, for drama (Caravaggio and followers).
notes.analogy: A dimmer switch vs a torch in a dark room.

notes.front: What is sfumato?
notes.back: Leonardo's smoky blending of tones and edges 'without lines', especially around eyes and mouth (Mona Lisa). Needs slow-drying oil glazes.
notes.analogy: A face seen through thin smoke: no outline, only soft transitions.

notes.front: In one-point perspective, what are the horizon line and the vanishing point?
notes.back: Horizon = the viewer's eye level. Vanishing point = the spot on it where all lines running into depth (orthogonals) converge.
notes.extra: History: Brunelleschi demonstrated it c. 1415, Alberti wrote the recipe (1435), Masaccio's Trinity is the first great painted example.

notes.front: What does the height of the vanishing point tell you?
notes.back: Where the painter put you. Low horizon: you look up, figures loom (monumental). High horizon: you survey the scene from above (maps, Bruegel's crowds).

notes.front: Linear vs atmospheric perspective?
notes.back: Linear: geometry, converging lines, shrinking size. Atmospheric: distant things get paler, bluer, softer and lower in contrast because of the air between.

notes.front: What is foreshortening?
notes.back: Drawing a form that points toward the viewer so it looks compressed: Mantegna's Dead Christ seen feet-first. The showpiece test of perspective skill.

notes.front: What is iconography?
notes.back: The study of subject matter and symbols: who the figures are and what objects mean (keys = Peter, lily = purity, skull = mortality). Read it before judging style.

notes.front: How do you identify a saint in pre-modern Western art?
notes.back: By a fixed attribute from their life or martyrdom: Peter keys, Catherine a wheel, Jerome a lion and red hat, Sebastian arrows, Mary Magdalene an ointment jar.
notes.analogy: Like a superhero's costume: the object, not the face, tells you who it is.

notes.front: What is vanitas / memento mori imagery?
notes.back: Reminders of death and the emptiness of worldly things: skulls, snuffed candles, hourglasses, rotting fruit, soap bubbles. Peaks in 17th-c. Dutch still life.

notes.front: What is contrapposto?
notes.back: Weight on one leg, hips and shoulders tilted in opposite directions, giving an S-curve. Greek invention c. 480 BC; the Western formula for a relaxed standing figure.

notes.front: Form vs content in analysing a work?
notes.back: Form: how it is made (line, colour, composition, scale, material). Content: what it shows and means (subject, iconography, context). Do form first, then meaning.

notes.front: What is the picture plane, and why does its treatment date a work?
notes.back: The imaginary window surface. Renaissance to 1860s: a window to look through. Modernism: flatness reasserted, the surface itself is the object.
notes.analogy: A glass pane: Renaissance painters wiped it clean to see through; modernists painted on the glass.

notes.text: A {{c1::triptych}} is a three-panel altarpiece whose wings fold shut; the {{c2::predella}} is the strip of small narrative scenes along its base.

notes.front: What is hierarchical scale, and what does its presence suggest?
notes.back: Size signals importance, not distance: pharaoh towers over servants, Christ over donors. Its presence points to Egyptian, medieval or non-Western conventions, not naturalism.

notes.front: Linear vs painterly handling (Wölfflin)?
notes.back: Linear: crisp contours, form defined by line (Botticelli, Ingres). Painterly: form built from patches of colour, edges merge, brushwork visible (Titian, Velázquez, Impressionists).

notes.front: How does buon fresco work, and why does it last?
notes.back: Water-ground pigment painted onto wet lime plaster; as the lime cures it locks the pigment into the wall. Done in daily patches (giornate); no corrections possible.
notes.analogy: Writing in wet concrete: permanent, but you must finish before it sets.

notes.front: Buon fresco vs fresco secco?
notes.back: Buon: on wet plaster, chemically bound, durable. Secco: on dry plaster with a binder, allows detail and blues (azurite) but flakes.
notes.extra: Pitfall: Leonardo's Last Supper used experimental secco-like methods on a dry wall and began decaying within decades.

notes.front: What is egg tempera, and how does it look?
notes.back: Pigment bound with egg yolk on a gesso panel; dries in seconds, so forms are built from fine hatched strokes. Bright, matte, crisp, but no soft blending or deep darks.
notes.extra: Anchors: Giotto, Fra Angelico, Botticelli. Standard in Italy before c. 1470.

notes.front: Why did oil paint displace tempera in the 15th century?
notes.back: Slow drying allows blending, translucent glazes, deep saturated darks, soft edges and reworking. Perfected in Flanders (van Eyck), then adopted in Venice.
notes.analogy: Tempera is a pen; oil is a pencil with an eraser.

notes.front: What is a glaze in oil painting?
notes.back: A thin translucent layer over a dry, lighter layer; light passes through and bounces back, giving glowing depth (van Eyck's reds, Titian's flesh).
notes.analogy: Coloured cellophane over a white page: the white shines through the colour.

notes.front: What is impasto, and what does it signal?
notes.back: Paint laid on thickly so brush or knife marks stand up (late Rembrandt, Van Gogh). Shows the maker's hand; impossible in tempera or fresco.

notes.front: Why did painting on canvas take off in Venice?
notes.back: Damp sea air ruined frescoes and warped panels; canvas was light, cheap, could be huge and rolled for shipping. From Titian's Venice it became the European norm.

notes.front: What is gesso, and why does it matter for early panels?
notes.back: A white chalk-and-glue ground on wood, sanded smooth: a luminous base for tempera and a bed for gold leaf. A glowing early panel implies gesso underneath.

notes.front: Why did gold-leaf backgrounds disappear c. 1400–1450?
notes.back: Naturalism: blue skies and landscapes replaced heaven's flat gold, and Alberti told painters to represent gold with paint rather than apply it.
notes.extra: Dating tip: gold ground = medieval or early Renaissance (or deliberate revival).

notes.front: Relief vs intaglio printmaking?
notes.back: Relief (woodcut): cut away the blanks, ink the raised surface. Intaglio (engraving, etching): ink sits in grooves in a metal plate and damp paper is pressed in to lift it.
notes.analogy: A rubber stamp vs a signet ring pressed into wax.

notes.front: Engraving vs etching?
notes.back: Engraving: lines cut by hand with a burin; controlled, swelling, formal (Dürer). Etching: drawn through a wax ground, bitten by acid; free and sketch-like (Rembrandt, Goya).

notes.front: Why did printmaking matter for the history of style?
notes.back: First reproducible images: compositions travelled across Europe (Dürer; Raphael via Marcantonio), artists became famous beyond their city, and later Japanese prints reached Paris.
notes.analogy: The internet of the 1500s: one design, thousands of copies, no borders.

notes.front: What did the collapsible tin paint tube (1841) make possible?
notes.back: Portable, premixed, long-lasting oil paint, so painters could finish outdoors (plein air). A precondition for Impressionism.
notes.extra: Quote: Renoir: 'Without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism.'

notes.front: How did 19th-c. synthetic pigments change painting?
notes.back: Cheap, bright, stable colours (chrome yellow, cobalt blue, viridian, synthetic ultramarine, later cadmiums) made the Impressionist and Fauvist palettes affordable.
notes.extra: Before: real ultramarine was ground lapis lazuli, costlier than gold, so contracts specified how much blue the Virgin's robe would get.

notes.front: Why do Impressionist paintings look so bright technically?
notes.back: White grounds instead of brown, high-key pure colours side by side (optical mixing), and little or no black. Academic paintings were built up from a dark ground.

notes.front: Lost-wax bronze casting: the basic idea?
notes.back: Model in wax over a clay core, coat in clay, heat so the wax runs out, pour bronze into the void, break the mould. Yields hollow, thin, light sculptures.

notes.front: Why can bronze figures stand in poses that marble cannot?
notes.back: Bronze is strong in tension and hollow; marble is heavy and snaps under tension, so outstretched arms need struts and tree-trunk props.
notes.extra: Tip: a tree stump beside a Greek-looking marble usually means a Roman copy of a lost bronze.

notes.front: Carving vs modelling in sculpture: how do they differ in logic?
notes.back: Carving (marble, wood) is subtractive: remove until the figure appears; mistakes are final. Modelling (clay, wax) is additive and revisable, then cast in bronze.
notes.analogy: Carving is editing a text down; modelling is drafting it up.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What do Palaeolithic cave paintings (Chauvet, Lascaux) show, and what is missing?
notes.back: Large animals in profile (horses, bison, aurochs), hand stencils and abstract signs, often using bulges in the rock. Almost no landscape and few humans.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: How do you recognise a Palaeolithic 'Venus' figurine (Willendorf)?
notes.back: Hand-sized, with exaggerated breasts, belly and hips and no face or feet. Reading: fertility or survival emphasis, but the meaning is unknown.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What is the Egyptian canon of figure representation?
notes.back: Composite view: head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders frontal, both feet flat, proportions from a grid. Each part shown in its most legible form, not as seen.
notes.analogy: An engineering drawing: plan and elevation combined so every part is unambiguous.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: Why did Egyptian art change so little over 3,000 years?
notes.back: Its job was religious and funerary: images had to be complete, legible and permanent to serve the dead for eternity. Innovation was a defect.
notes.extra: Exception: the Amarna episode under Akhenaten, which proves the canon was a choice.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What tells you a figure is a pharaoh or god in Egyptian art?
notes.back: Hierarchical scale, rigid idealised frontality, and attributes (double crown, crook and flail, false beard). Servants and workers are small and lively.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What was the Amarna style?
notes.back: Akhenaten's short break (c. 1350 BC): elongated skulls, sagging bellies, intimate family scenes, rays of the sun-disc Aten. Reversed immediately after his death.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: Ziggurat vs pyramid?
notes.back: Ziggurat: Mesopotamian stepped mud-brick platform with a temple on top, an artificial mountain for the god. Pyramid: Egyptian stone tomb.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: How do you recognise a Sumerian votive statue (Tell Asmar)?
notes.back: Huge inlaid staring eyes, hands clasped at the chest, cylindrical body, fleecy skirt. A stand-in that prays to the god on the donor's behalf, forever.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What narrative habit do the Standard of Ur and the Stele of Hammurabi share?
notes.back: Scenes stacked in horizontal registers read like a strip, with hierarchical scale and the ruler receiving authority from a god.

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: What are Assyrian lamassu and palace reliefs for?
notes.back: Royal propaganda: colossal human-headed winged bulls guard the gates, and low reliefs of lion hunts and sieges exalt the king's power (Nimrud, Nineveh).

notes.deck: Art History::03 Prehistoric & Ancient Near East
notes.front: Minoan vs Egyptian wall painting: how to tell?
notes.back: Minoan (Knossos): fluid curves, movement, dolphins and bull-leapers, no grid. Egyptian: rigid composite figures in registers. Minoan is the playful one.

notes.front: Greek art in one line: Archaic → Classical → Hellenistic?
notes.back: Stiff frontal kouroi → idealised, balanced, living bodies (5th c. BC) → emotional, twisting, theatrical figures after Alexander. Naturalism rises, idealism peaks, then drama.

notes.front: How do you recognise an Archaic kouros?
notes.back: Rigid frontal stance, left foot forward, arms at sides, patterned hair, the 'Archaic smile'. An Egyptian pose made nude and free-standing.

notes.front: What changed with the Kritios Boy (c. 480 BC)?
notes.back: First contrapposto: weight on one leg, hips and shoulders counter-tilted, head turned. The body shown as a living mechanism, not a symbol. Start of Classical sculpture.

notes.front: What is the Classical ideal (Polykleitos' Doryphoros)?
notes.back: Mathematically proportioned, idealised, calm body in contrapposto; no individual emotion. Beauty as measurable harmony (symmetria).

notes.front: Classical vs Hellenistic sculpture: how to tell?
notes.back: Classical: calm, idealised, youthful, self-contained. Hellenistic: twisting, emotional, theatrical; old age, pain, children, drunkards (Laocoön, Dying Gaul, Nike of Samothrace).
notes.analogy: A portrait photo vs a sports-action shot.

notes.text: The three Greek orders: {{c1::Doric}} (no base, plain cushion capital, sturdy), {{c2::Ionic}} (base, scroll volutes, slender) and {{c3::Corinthian}} (acanthus-leaf capital, the Roman favourite).

notes.front: What are the Parthenon's optical refinements, and why?
notes.back: Columns lean slightly inward and swell (entasis), the platform curves upward, corner columns are thicker. They counter optical illusions so the building looks perfectly straight.
notes.analogy: Kerning in typography: you cheat the geometry so the eye sees even spacing.

notes.front: Black-figure vs red-figure vase painting?
notes.back: Black-figure: figures painted in black slip, details scratched in. Red-figure (c. 530 BC): background painted black, figures left red and drawn with a brush, allowing fluid anatomy.
notes.extra: Why vases matter: Greek panel and wall painting is lost; fired pottery survives.

notes.front: Why are most 'Greek' statues in museums actually Roman?
notes.back: Greek bronzes were melted down for metal; Romans made marble copies for villas and baths. Hence the struts and tree trunks, and our view of Polykleitos through copies.

notes.front: What is distinctively Roman about Republican portraiture?
notes.back: Verism: wrinkles, warts, bald heads shown unflinchingly, honouring age and gravitas. Imperial portraits (Augustus of Prima Porta) swing back to Greek idealism.

notes.front: What did Roman architecture add that Greek lacked?
notes.back: Concrete, the arch, the vault and the dome: the Pantheon, Colosseum, aqueducts. Greek post-and-lintel limited spans; Roman concrete enclosed vast interiors.

notes.front: How does the Pantheon's 43 m concrete dome stand?
notes.back: Massive drum walls, aggregate that gets lighter toward the top (pumice near the oculus), coffers that remove weight, and an oculus where no material is needed.
notes.analogy: A well-engineered eggshell: thick where the load is, thin where it isn't.

notes.front: What is Trajan's Column an example of?
notes.back: Continuous narrative: one spiralling relief tells the Dacian wars scene after scene. Roman state storytelling, later a model for medieval and Renaissance cycles.

notes.front: Why do the Pompeian wall-painting styles matter?
notes.back: They prove Romans had illusionistic painting: fake marble, architectural vistas with intuitive perspective, still life, landscape. The skill was lost and rediscovered in the Renaissance.

notes.front: Greek vs Roman temple: how to tell?
notes.back: Greek: freestanding on low steps, colonnade all round. Roman (Maison Carrée): on a high podium, strongly frontal with a deep porch, columns engaged in the side walls.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Why did late Roman and early Christian art abandon naturalism?
notes.back: The job changed from showing bodies to conveying spiritual truth: frontal, flat, big-eyed, weightless figures on gold communicate the divine better than illusion. A choice, not lost skill.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: How do you recognise Byzantine art?
notes.back: Gold mosaic grounds, frontal elongated figures with huge eyes, no cast shadows, stylised drapery, hierarchical placement (Pantokrator in the dome). Ravenna, Hagia Sophia, icons.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What is an icon, and why does its style barely change?
notes.back: A sacred panel of Christ, Mary or a saint, venerated as a window onto the holy. Fidelity to the prototype matters more than invention, so the style stays stable for centuries.
notes.analogy: A protocol spec: the value is in everyone implementing it identically, not in creativity.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What was Iconoclasm (726–843) and its lasting effect?
notes.back: Byzantine ban and destruction of religious images. Afterwards images were defended as windows, not idols, and large sculpture stayed suspect in the East while it flourished in the West.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: How does Hagia Sophia (537) carry its dome?
notes.back: On pendentives: curved triangles that turn a square bay into a circle, with a ring of windows at the base so the dome seems to float on light.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What characterises Insular manuscripts (Book of Kells, Lindisfarne)?
notes.back: Dense interlace, spirals, animal knots, carpet pages, giant decorated initials. Celtic-Germanic abstract ornament absorbing Christianity; no interest in naturalism.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What did Carolingian art attempt?
notes.back: Charlemagne's revival (c. 800) of Roman models: classical figure types, naturalistic drapery, basilica plans, and a clear new script. A first 'renaissance'.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: How do you recognise Romanesque architecture?
notes.back: Thick walls, small windows, round arches, barrel and groin vaults, heavy piers, dark fortress-like interiors (Durham, Vézelay, Speyer).

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Why were Romanesque walls so thick and windows so small?
notes.back: A stone vault pushes outward; without external buttresses the wall itself must absorb the thrust, and every opening weakens it.
notes.analogy: A dam: you cannot cut windows in it without it bursting.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What is a Romanesque tympanum about (Autun, Vézelay, Conques)?
notes.back: The sculpted half-circle over the portal, usually a Last Judgment or Christ in Majesty: it frightens and instructs pilgrims as they enter. Monumental stone sculpture reborn after 500 years.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What is the Romanesque figure style?
notes.back: Elongated, stylised, drapery in rhythmic lines, bodies bent to fit the architectural frame, hierarchical scale, expressive rather than natural (Gislebertus at Autun).

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.text: Gothic structure rests on three innovations: the {{c1::pointed arch}} (any height, steeper thrust), the {{c2::ribbed vault}} (load channelled to piers) and the {{c3::flying buttress}} (thrust carried outside the wall).

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Why does the pointed arch beat the round arch?
notes.back: It directs thrust more steeply downward and can reach any height over any span, so bays of different widths share one vault height. A round arch's height is fixed at half its span.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What did the flying buttress enable visually?
notes.back: Walls freed from carrying load became screens of stained glass: tall, skeletal, light-flooded interiors (Chartres, Amiens, Sainte-Chapelle).
notes.extra: Idea: Abbot Suger at Saint-Denis (1144) made light itself the metaphor for God; the engineering served theology.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Romanesque vs Gothic: how to tell at a glance?
notes.back: Romanesque: round arches, thick walls, small windows, horizontal mass. Gothic: pointed arches, huge windows, verticality, flying buttresses, pinnacles.
notes.analogy: A bunker vs a greenhouse.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: How does Gothic sculpture change from Romanesque?
notes.back: Figures detach from the wall, gain natural proportions and weight, gentle smiles and a swaying S-curve (Reims, Naumburg). The sacred becomes human.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: What is International Gothic (c. 1375–1425)?
notes.back: Courtly, elegant, decorative: elongated graceful figures, rich fabrics, gold, minutely observed animals and plants but no real space (Limbourg brothers, Gentile da Fabriano, Wilton Diptych).

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Why is Giotto (Arena Chapel, c. 1305) called the start of Western painting?
notes.back: Solid, weighty figures in believable space, real emotion, consistent light, blue skies instead of gold. Painting became human drama; Byzantine flatness was abandoned.

notes.deck: Art History::05 Medieval: Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic
notes.front: Giotto (Florence) vs Duccio and Simone Martini (Siena)?
notes.back: Florence: mass, volume, drama, plainness. Siena: line, grace, gold, Byzantine refinement. Florence leads to the Renaissance; Siena feeds International Gothic.

notes.front: What is the core shift from Gothic to Renaissance?
notes.back: Humanism: man as the measure; antiquity revived (anatomy, proportion, the orders); rational space via perspective; artists as named individuals with theory. Florence, c. 1400.

notes.front: What did Brunelleschi's dome (1420–36) prove?
notes.back: A dome wider than the Pantheon's could be built without wooden centering: double shell, herringbone brickwork, pointed profile. Engineering plus classical ambition.

notes.front: Why does Masaccio's Trinity (c. 1427) matter?
notes.back: First painting in coherent one-point perspective: the chapel seems hollowed into the wall. Giotto's weight plus consistent light. The blueprint for a century.

notes.front: What did Donatello's bronze David break?
notes.back: The first free-standing nude since antiquity: life-size, contrapposto, sensual. Classical sculpture reclaimed for a biblical subject.

notes.front: What marks Early Renaissance Florence (Botticelli) as against the High Renaissance?
notes.back: Line over volume: crisp contours, graceful decorative rhythm, pale flat colour, Neoplatonic myth (Birth of Venus). High Renaissance replaces line with sfumato and mass.

notes.front: What marks the High Renaissance (c. 1495–1520)?
notes.back: Harmony, balance, idealisation, grandeur: pyramidal compositions, unified light, figures at ease yet monumental. Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo, Bramante; Rome takes over from Florence.

notes.front: What did Leonardo contribute that his peers didn't?
notes.back: Sfumato and atmospheric unity, psychological expression, anatomy from dissection: painting treated as a science (Last Supper, Mona Lisa).

notes.front: What makes Raphael's School of Athens the High Renaissance textbook?
notes.back: Perfect perspective architecture, balanced groups, every pose graceful, pagan philosophy harmonised with a papal library. Clarity and effortless grace.

notes.front: What is Michelangelo's conception of sculpture?
notes.back: Freeing the figure already inside the marble; the body as vehicle of spirit, with terribilità (awesome force). David (1504); the Sistine ceiling painted as if sculpted.
notes.extra: Lead-on: his twisting figura serpentinata and the Last Judgment's crowding feed straight into Mannerism.

notes.front: Florence/Rome vs Venice in the 16th century: disegno vs colorito?
notes.back: Florence: drawing, contour, form, intellect (Michelangelo). Venice: colour, light, texture, mood, oil on canvas (Giorgione, Titian). The root of the linear-vs-painterly split.

notes.front: What did Titian change about oil painting?
notes.back: Loose visible brushwork and glazes built up on canvas, forms emerging from colour rather than line; late works almost abstract. The model for Rubens, Velázquez and Rembrandt.

notes.front: What is distinctive about the Northern Renaissance (Flanders)?
notes.back: Oil glazes, microscopic detail of textures and reflections, sacred symbolism hidden in domestic settings, empirical rather than mathematical perspective (van Eyck, Campin, van der Weyden).

notes.front: Italian vs Northern Renaissance: how to tell?
notes.back: Italian: idealised nudes, classical architecture, geometric perspective, fresco and tempera. Northern: realism of surfaces, interiors, Gothic details, oil on panel, clothed figures and symbolic objects.
notes.analogy: Italian painters built the scene from geometry outward; Northern painters from the texture of each object inward.

notes.front: What is the 'disguised symbolism' of van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434)?
notes.back: Everyday objects carry sacred meaning: one lit candle (God's presence), the dog (fidelity), shoes removed (holy ground), a mirror framed by Passion scenes.

notes.front: How do you recognise Bosch?
notes.back: Crowded fantastical landscapes of hybrid monsters, sin and punishment: a late-medieval moral imagination in Renaissance oil (Garden of Earthly Delights). Not Surrealism, though Surrealists adopted him.

notes.front: Why did Dürer matter beyond Germany?
notes.back: He fused Northern detail with Italian theory (proportion, perspective) and raised woodcut and engraving to fine art, reaching all Europe (Apocalypse, Melencolia I).

notes.front: How did the Reformation change Northern art?
notes.back: Iconoclasm and suspicion of religious images pushed painters to portraiture, landscape, genre and still life (Holbein, Bruegel). The seed of Dutch Golden Age specialisation.

notes.front: What is Bruegel the Elder about?
notes.back: Peasant life, seasons and proverbs in panoramic landscapes seen from above; humanity small, busy and comic. No altarpieces, nothing Italian in the bodies.

notes.text: Alberti's On Painting (1435) defined a picture as an open {{c1::window}} through which a story is seen; this idea rules Western painting until {{c2::Manet}} reasserts the flat surface.

notes.front: What is a sacra conversazione, and what does it signal?
notes.back: Madonna and saints sharing one unified space and light instead of separate gold panels. Renaissance unity replacing the Gothic polyptych.

notes.front: Why is the Renaissance nude significant?
notes.back: The classical body revived as the vehicle of ideal beauty and anatomical knowledge (Donatello, Michelangelo, Titian's Venus of Urbino). Medieval nudes were only Adam, Eve and the damned.

notes.front: What is Mannerism (c. 1520–1600) reacting to?
notes.back: Raphael and Michelangelo had perfected harmony; the next generation pursued maniera (stylishness) instead: elongation, twisting poses, acid colour, compressed space, deliberate artifice.
notes.analogy: After a language is standardised, the next generation writes in slang and ornament to prove virtuosity.

notes.front: How do you recognise a Mannerist painting?
notes.back: Tiny heads on long necks and limbs, serpentine twists, unstable crowded compositions, lurid pink-green-violet, irrational scale (Parmigianino's Madonna with the Long Neck, Pontormo, Bronzino).

notes.front: What is distinctive about El Greco?
notes.back: Flame-like elongated figures, cold flickering light, ecstatic spirituality, Byzantine icon training under Venetian colour (Burial of the Count of Orgaz). Spanish Mannerism; later loved by Expressionists.

notes.front: Why did the Baroque arise around 1600?
notes.back: The Counter-Reformation wanted art that was clear, direct and emotionally overwhelming, and absolutist courts wanted grandeur. A reaction against Mannerist obscurity.

notes.front: How do you recognise Baroque painting?
notes.back: Dramatic diagonals, strong light–dark, movement caught mid-action, emotional intensity, theatricality, rich colour, the viewer pulled into the scene.

notes.front: What did Caravaggio change?
notes.back: Sacred scenes played by dirty-footed street models under a tenebrist spotlight, at the instant of crisis (Calling of St Matthew). No idealisation; copied across Europe by the Caravaggisti.

notes.front: What is Baroque about Bernini's Ecstasy of St Teresa?
notes.back: Marble turned into cloth, flesh and cloud; a frozen climax; a hidden window and gilt rays; the chapel staged as theatre with sculpted spectators. Sculpture, architecture and light fused.

notes.front: Rubens vs Poussin: what was the 'colour vs line' quarrel?
notes.back: Rubens: colour, flesh, swirling energy (Venetian heritage). Poussin: drawing, order, stoic clarity (classical Baroque). The same fight returns as Delacroix vs Ingres.

notes.front: Why does Dutch 17th-century art look so different from Italian Baroque?
notes.back: A Protestant republic with no church commissions and a wealthy merchant market: small easel pictures of portraits, landscape, genre and still life for homes, by specialists per genre.
notes.analogy: A B2C market instead of a few enterprise clients: many small sales shape the product.

notes.front: What is distinctive about Rembrandt?
notes.back: Psychological depth, golden light out of darkness, rough impasto in late work, self-portraits charting ageing, master etcher. Baroque drama made inward (Night Watch, Prodigal Son).

notes.front: What is distinctive about Vermeer?
notes.back: Quiet domestic interiors lit from a left window, pearly light, dotted highlights, precise optics (camera obscura debated), stillness. Only about 35 paintings.

notes.front: Why is Velázquez's Las Meninas so admired by painters?
notes.back: Loose brushwork that resolves at a distance; a puzzle of mirror, viewer and painter inside the picture; dignity for everyone from princess to dwarf. Manet: 'the painter of painters'.

notes.front: What is a Baroque illusionistic ceiling (quadratura, di sotto in sù)?
notes.back: Painted architecture continuing the real building, with figures soaring into an open sky seen from below (Pozzo's Sant'Ignazio). The ceiling dissolved: Baroque as theatre.

notes.front: How do you recognise Rococo (c. 1720–1780)?
notes.back: Pastel pinks and blues, asymmetric C- and S-curves, shells and gilt, playful eroticism, aristocratic leisure, small intimate scale (Watteau, Boucher, Fragonard's Swing).

notes.front: Baroque vs Rococo: how to tell?
notes.back: Baroque: grand, dramatic, religious or royal, dark-light contrasts, heavy. Rococo: intimate, light-hearted, pastel, erotic, decorative, for the salon. Rococo is Baroque gone private after Louis XIV (1715).
notes.analogy: A cathedral organ vs a harpsichord in a boudoir.

notes.front: What did Rococo react against, and what reacted against it?
notes.back: Against the pompous grandeur of Versailles. Then Enlightenment moralists (Diderot) attacked it as frivolous, preparing the austerity of Neoclassicism.

notes.front: Why does Chardin stand apart in Rococo France?
notes.back: Humble still lifes and quiet servants in thick, sober paint; moral seriousness amid frivolity. A bridge from Dutch genre painting to Cézanne.

notes.front: What triggered Neoclassicism (c. 1760–1830)?
notes.back: Excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii, Winckelmann's praise of Greek 'noble simplicity and calm grandeur', Enlightenment reason, and revolutionary politics wanting Roman virtue.

notes.front: How do you recognise Neoclassical painting?
notes.back: Frieze-like rows of figures in a shallow stage space, clear outlines, smooth invisible brushwork, sober colour, Greek or Roman subjects of civic virtue (David's Oath of the Horatii).

notes.front: What is the point of Ingres' style?
notes.back: Line as supreme: flawless contour and surface, idealised even at anatomical cost (the extra vertebrae of La Grande Odalisque). The academic standard Delacroix fought.

notes.front: What is Romanticism (c. 1790–1850) reacting against?
notes.back: Enlightenment rationalism and Neoclassical rules. It prizes emotion, imagination, the sublime, nature's power, the exotic, the medieval and the individual.

notes.front: How do you recognise Romantic painting?
notes.back: Dramatic diagonals, loose brushwork, saturated colour, storms, shipwrecks, ruins, the Orient, extreme emotion, a lone figure against vast nature (Géricault, Delacroix, Turner, Friedrich).

notes.front: Neoclassicism vs Romanticism: how to tell?
notes.back: Neoclassical: line, smooth, calm, antique subject, moral clarity (Ingres). Romantic: colour, rough, turbulent, contemporary or exotic subject, feeling (Delacroix).
notes.analogy: A formal proof vs a thunderstorm.

notes.front: What is the sublime?
notes.back: Awe mixed with terror before overwhelming nature or vastness (Burke, Kant). Beauty pleases; the sublime overwhelms. Friedrich's tiny figures in fog, Turner's storms.

notes.front: What did Goya do that was new?
notes.back: Horror without heroism: Third of May 1808, Disasters of War, the Black Paintings, The Sleep of Reason. From court painter to modern conscience; no comfort offered.

notes.front: Why is Turner called a proto-Impressionist?
notes.back: His late work dissolves objects into light, colour and weather (Rain, Steam and Speed); atmosphere is the subject. Monet and Pissarro studied him in London in 1870.

notes.front: Constable vs Turner?
notes.back: Constable: humble English countryside, scientifically studied clouds, fresh outdoor sketches, truth to place. Turner: sublime drama, dissolving light, exotic travel. Both freed the brush.

notes.front: What is Realism (c. 1840–1880) reacting against?
notes.back: Both Neoclassical idealism and Romantic melodrama: paint contemporary ordinary life, workers and peasants, life-size, unflattered (Courbet, Millet, Daumier). Political after 1848.

notes.front: Why was Courbet's Burial at Ornans (1850) a scandal?
notes.back: History-painting scale and gravity given to a provincial funeral of nobodies: no hero, no idealisation, dull faces. It overturned the academic hierarchy of genres.

notes.front: What was the academic hierarchy of genres?
notes.back: History painting (biblical, mythological, heroic) at the top; then portrait, genre scenes, landscape, and still life at the bottom. The 19th-c. avant-garde inverted it.

notes.front: What was the Paris Salon, and why does it matter for modern art?
notes.back: The annual state exhibition juried by the Academy, the only route to buyers. Rejections (Manet, the Impressionists) led to the Salon des Refusés (1863) and independent shows: the dealer-gallery system was born.
notes.analogy: An app store with one gatekeeper; the rejected built their own distribution.

notes.front: What did the Pre-Raphaelites (1848) want?
notes.back: To reject post-Raphael academic convention: brilliant colour, minute natural detail, medieval and literary subjects, moral seriousness (Millais' Ophelia, Rossetti). A Romantic-Realist hybrid in Britain.

notes.front: How did photography (1839) change painting's job?
notes.back: It took over likeness and documentation, so painters moved to what cameras couldn't do: colour, perception, feeling, form. It also supplied odd cropping and frozen motion (Degas).

notes.front: Why is Manet the pivot to modern painting?
notes.back: Flattened forms, visible brushwork, harsh frontal light, contemporary subjects staring back at the viewer (Olympia, Déjeuner sur l'herbe, 1863). The picture plane reasserted; painting about painting.

notes.front: What did Impressionism aim to capture?
notes.back: The fleeting impression: light and colour at one moment, painted outdoors with broken strokes and no black. Subjects: modern leisure, Paris, railways, suburbs.
notes.extra: Name: from Monet's Impression, Sunrise, mocked by a critic at the first independent show in 1874.

notes.front: How do you recognise an Impressionist painting?
notes.back: Short visible strokes, pure colours side by side, blue-violet shadows, no outlines, high-key palette, casual cropping, everyday modern scenes.

notes.text: Impressionism depended on {{c1::paint tubes}} (portable oil paint), {{c2::synthetic pigments}} (bright and cheap), {{c3::railways}} (day trips to the Seine) and the example of photography.

notes.front: Why did Impressionists paint shadows blue and violet?
notes.back: Shadows are lit by the sky and take the complement of the sunlit colour; they recorded the colour sensation, not the object's 'local' colour. Critics used to brown shadows were shocked.

notes.front: What is Monet's series method about (Haystacks, Rouen Cathedral)?
notes.back: One motif at different hours and seasons to show that the real subject is light, not the object. Leads toward abstraction and ends in the Water Lilies.

notes.front: Degas vs Monet: two Impressionisms?
notes.back: Degas: indoors, artificial light, drawing, bodies (dancers, bathers), viewpoints from photography and Japanese prints; disliked plein air. Monet: outdoor light on landscape. Same exhibitions, opposite methods.

notes.front: What is Post-Impressionism (c. 1885–1910)?
notes.back: Not a style but a shared reaction: Impressionism felt too fleeting and formless, so each artist restored something: structure (Cézanne), emotion (Van Gogh), symbol (Gauguin), science (Seurat).

notes.front: What was Cézanne trying to do?
notes.back: 'Make of Impressionism something solid and durable like the art of the museums': form built from patches of colour, slight multiple viewpoints, underlying geometry (Mont Sainte-Victoire). Father of Cubism.

notes.front: Seurat's pointillism: the idea?
notes.back: Tiny dots of pure, often complementary colour meant to mix in the eye for extra luminosity, inside rigidly ordered compositions (La Grande Jatte). Impressionism made scientific.
notes.analogy: Pixels: the image forms only at viewing distance.

notes.front: What carries the emotion in Van Gogh?
notes.back: Thick impasto, directional swirling strokes, heightened arbitrary colour (yellow against blue) expressing feeling rather than optics. The precursor of Expressionism.

notes.front: What did Gauguin reject?
notes.back: Western naturalism and the city: flat zones of bold colour with dark outlines (cloisonnism), 'primitive' Brittany and Tahiti, symbolic meaning. Precursor of Fauvism and Primitivism.

notes.front: How did Japanese ukiyo-e prints (Japonisme) change Western painting?
notes.back: Flat colour areas, bold outlines, asymmetric cropping, high viewpoints, everyday subjects, no shadow modelling: seen in Manet, Degas, Van Gogh, Toulouse-Lautrec and Art Nouveau.

notes.front: What is Symbolism (1880s–90s)?
notes.back: A reaction against Realist and Impressionist materialism: dreams, myth, the inner world, suggestive colour (Moreau, Redon, Munch's Scream). Feeds Expressionism and Surrealism.

notes.front: What did Rodin do to sculpture?
notes.back: Rough unfinished surfaces, fragments, movement and emotion over polish (Burghers of Calais, The Thinker); expressive modelling after academic smoothness. Sculpture's Impressionist.

notes.front: What is Art Nouveau (c. 1890–1910)?
notes.back: Whiplash organic curves, plant forms, flat decorative line, unity of all the arts (posters, glass, buildings): Mucha, Horta, Gaudí, Klimt's Vienna. Rejected historicism; killed by WWI and the machine aesthetic.

notes.front: What is Fauvism (1905–08)?
notes.back: Matisse, Derain: wild colour freed from nature (a green stripe down a face), flat patterns, Gauguin and Van Gogh pushed further. 'Wild beasts'. Brief, but colour was now autonomous.

notes.front: Fauvism vs Expressionism: how to tell?
notes.back: Fauvism (France): colour for joy, harmony, decoration. Expressionism (Germany): distorted colour and form for anxiety, angst and spiritual urgency; jagged lines, woodcut revival.

notes.front: Die Brücke vs Der Blaue Reiter?
notes.back: Brücke (Dresden 1905; Kirchner, Nolde): raw, jagged, urban angst, primitivism, woodcuts. Blaue Reiter (Munich 1911; Kandinsky, Marc, Klee): lyrical, spiritual, colour symbolism, toward abstraction.

notes.front: What did Cubism (1907–14) reject, and propose instead?
notes.back: Rejected the single fixed viewpoint of Renaissance perspective: objects shown from several angles at once as faceted planes on a shallow surface. Picasso and Braque, out of Cézanne and African masks.
notes.analogy: A 3D model unfolded into a UV map: all sides laid flat on one sheet.

notes.front: Analytic vs Synthetic Cubism?
notes.back: Analytic (1909–12): near-monochrome browns and greys, objects shattered into facets, barely readable. Synthetic (1912–14): rebuilt from flat shapes, bright colour, collage with newspaper and wallpaper.

notes.front: Why does Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) matter?
notes.back: It broke anatomy and space: mask-like faces from Iberian and African sources, angular bodies, no depth. The shock that launched Cubism; the body as construction, not beauty.

notes.front: Why was collage (1912) radical?
notes.back: Real materials (newspaper, oilcloth) glued onto the picture break the illusion contract: the picture is an object, not a window. Leads to Dada montage and assemblage.

notes.front: What is Futurism (1909–16)?
notes.back: Italian cult of speed, machines, the city and even war: Cubist fragmentation plus motion lines and repeated forms (Boccioni's Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, Balla). Ended by WWI and fascist ties.

notes.front: What is abstraction, and who reached it first (c. 1910–15)?
notes.back: Painting with no depicted object. Kandinsky (colour as music), Malevich (Black Square, 1915), Mondrian (grids). Hilma af Klint earlier, but unseen.

notes.front: Kandinsky vs Mondrian: two roads to abstraction?
notes.back: Kandinsky: expressive, lyrical, biomorphic, colour as music. Mondrian: geometric, reductive, verticals, horizontals and primaries as universal harmony. Hot vs cold abstraction.

notes.front: What is Malevich's Suprematism?
notes.back: Pure geometric shapes floating on white (Black Square, 1915): the 'zero of form', feeling freed from objects. Russian revolutionary utopia, later suppressed under Stalin.

notes.front: What is Constructivism?
notes.back: Post-1917 Russian art as engineering for the new society: geometry, industrial materials, posters, architecture (Tatlin's Tower, Rodchenko, Lissitzky). Art into production; a Bauhaus influence.

notes.front: What is Dada (1916–24)?
notes.back: Anti-art born of disgust at WWI: chance, nonsense, collage, photomontage, readymades, performance (Zurich's Cabaret Voltaire, Berlin, New York). It attacked skill and meaning themselves.

notes.front: What is the argument of Duchamp's Fountain (1917)?
notes.back: A signed urinal: the artist's choice and the gallery context make art, not craft. The foundation of Conceptual art; 'retinal' painting dismissed.

notes.front: What is Surrealism (1924–), and what fed it?
notes.back: Breton's programme to free the unconscious via Freud: dream imagery, automatism, chance, uncanny juxtapositions. Grew out of Dada but constructive, not nihilist.

notes.front: The two modes of Surrealist painting?
notes.back: Illusionistic: dream scenes in precise academic technique (Dalí, Magritte, Tanguy). Automatist: free biomorphic forms from chance and the hand (Miró, Masson, Ernst's frottage). The second led to Abstract Expressionism.

notes.front: What was the Bauhaus (1919–33)?
notes.back: German school uniting art, craft and industry: workshops, functional design, geometry, primaries, typography, tubular steel (Gropius, Klee, Kandinsky, Breuer). Closed by the Nazis, spread to the US.

notes.front: What is De Stijl (1917–31)?
notes.back: Dutch purism: straight lines, right angles, primaries plus black, white and grey, applied to painting, furniture and buildings (Mondrian, Rietveld's Schröder House and Red-Blue Chair). Universal harmony after war.

notes.front: What is Primitivism in modern art?
notes.back: Borrowing from African, Oceanic and folk art for simplified forms and expressive force (Gauguin, Picasso, Brücke, Modigliani). Enabled by colonial museums; now read critically as appropriation.

notes.front: Expressionism vs Cubism: what does each attack?
notes.back: Expressionism distorts colour and form for inner feeling and keeps the subject. Cubism dissects form and space and suppresses feeling and colour. Emotional vs intellectual revolt against naturalism.

notes.front: What is the avant-garde logic behind the rapid succession of -isms (1905–30)?
notes.back: Each movement defines itself against the last: value lies in rupture and novelty, and manifestos and exhibitions replace commissions.
notes.analogy: Framework churn: each release markets itself by what the previous one got wrong.

notes.front: Why is Brancusi important for sculpture?
notes.back: Radical simplification to essential ovoid and soaring forms, polished surfaces, truth to material, the base as part of the work (Bird in Space). From Rodin's modelling to pure form.

notes.front: Art Deco vs Bauhaus: how to tell?
notes.back: Deco: luxurious decorative geometry, zigzags, chrome, exotic materials (Chrysler Building). Bauhaus/International Style: austere, functional, no ornament. Both machine-age: glamour vs ethic.

notes.front: What is Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity)?
notes.back: German 1920s reaction against Expressionism: cold, sharp, satirical realism of Weimar society (Grosz, Dix, Schad). Part of the post-WWI 'return to order', like Picasso's neoclassical phase.

notes.front: What is Mexican Muralism?
notes.back: State-backed public frescoes of history and revolution (Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros, 1920s–50s): fresco revived for mass politics; influenced US WPA murals and Pollock's scale.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: Why did the centre of art shift to New York after 1945?
notes.back: European artists fled there (Surrealists, Mondrian, Bauhaus staff), Paris was exhausted, and the US had wealth, MoMA, critics like Greenberg, and Cold War cultural promotion.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is Abstract Expressionism (c. 1945–60)?
notes.back: Large non-representational painting as existential act: gestural action painting (Pollock, de Kooning) and contemplative colour field (Rothko, Newman). Surrealist automatism at mural scale.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: Action painting vs colour field?
notes.back: Action: energetic gesture, drips, slashes, a record of the body (Pollock, de Kooning). Colour field: large quiet expanses of colour for a sublime stillness (Rothko's rectangles, Newman's zips).

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What did Pollock's drip painting (1947) change?
notes.back: Canvas on the floor, paint poured from above: all-over composition with no focal point, the painting as a recorded event. Easel, brush and composition rejected.
notes.analogy: A seismograph trace: the image is the record of the movement, not a picture of something.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What was Greenberg's modernist argument?
notes.back: Each art should pursue what is unique to its medium; painting's essence is flatness and colour, so progress means purging illusion and story. Justified AbEx; attacked by Pop and Minimalism.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is Pop Art (c. 1955–70) reacting against?
notes.back: AbEx's heroic inwardness: it embraced advertising, comics, celebrity and packaging, using commercial techniques (silkscreen, Ben-Day dots). Warhol, Lichtenstein, Hamilton, Oldenburg.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is the point of Warhol's silkscreened Marilyns?
notes.back: Mechanical repetition erases the artist's hand and turns fame and death into consumable images; the Factory as anti-studio. Art as commodity, celebrated and critiqued at once.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: How do Johns and Rauschenberg bridge AbEx and Pop?
notes.back: Johns' Flags and Targets: painterly surface on a flat ready-made sign (is it a flag or a painting?). Rauschenberg's Combines: AbEx brushwork plus real junk. 'Neo-Dada'.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is Minimalism (1960s)?
notes.back: Industrial materials, repeated geometric units, no composition, expression or illusion: 'what you see is what you see' (Stella). Judd's boxes, Flavin's fluorescent tubes, Andre's floor plates.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: Minimalism vs Abstract Expressionism?
notes.back: AbEx: gesture, emotion, the artist's hand, painting. Minimalism: fabricated, impersonal, serial objects in real space. Both abstract, opposite about the self.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is Conceptual art (late 1960s–70s)?
notes.back: The idea is the work; execution is secondary or absent: instructions (LeWitt), language (Kosuth's One and Three Chairs), documents (Weiner). From Duchamp; against the art object as commodity.
notes.analogy: The source code is the work; any compiled binary is incidental.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What links Land art, Performance and Installation (1960s–70s)?
notes.back: 'Dematerialisation': escaping the gallery and the saleable object. Smithson's Spiral Jetty, Abramović's performances, Beuys' actions. Experience over artefact.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: What is Postmodernism in art (c. 1975–)?
notes.back: The end of belief in avant-garde progress: appropriation (Sherman, Koons), irony, pastiche of past styles, critique of originality and the museum. No single style; against Greenberg's purity.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: Why do Bacon and Freud matter in a post-war story dominated by abstraction?
notes.back: Figuration never died: Bacon's screaming distorted bodies and Freud's raw flesh carry existential angst in paint while New York went abstract. 'Progress' is only one narrative.

notes.deck: Art History::11 Post-war: AbEx to Conceptual
notes.front: How should you approach contemporary art after 1990?
notes.back: No dominant style; the medium is a choice (video, installation, photography, painting coexist); it is global (biennales) and about identity, politics and institutions. Read context and intention first.

notes.front: What matters most in Chinese literati ink painting?
notes.back: The brushstroke as the trace of the scholar-painter's character; calligraphy and painting share one brush and ink; empty space counts; landscape (shanshui) as philosophy, not a view.

notes.front: How does Chinese landscape space differ from Western perspective?
notes.back: Shifting viewpoints along a scroll, a high 'floating' vantage, distance by stacking and mist rather than converging lines. The viewer travels through, not looks through a window.
notes.analogy: A walk recorded in sequence, versus a snapshot from one spot.

notes.front: Why did China rank calligraphy above painting?
notes.back: Both are brush and ink, and calligraphy shows the purest trace of mind and hand. Painting was valued when it showed the same qualities; literati amateurs outranked court professionals.

notes.front: What are the 'Three Perfections' and the colophon tradition?
notes.back: Poetry, calligraphy and painting united on one scroll, with seals and later inscriptions (colophons) added by owners. The work accumulates responses over centuries.
notes.analogy: A document with a comment thread that stays part of the document forever.

notes.front: What is ukiyo-e?
notes.back: Japanese 'pictures of the floating world' (c. 1670–1880): woodblock prints of courtesans, kabuki actors and landscapes for urban Edo buyers (Hokusai's Great Wave, Hiroshige, Utamaro). Cheap mass-produced art.

notes.front: How was an ukiyo-e print made?
notes.back: A team: the designer draws, a carver cuts a key block and one block per colour, a printer rubs water-based colour onto paper with a baren, a publisher coordinates. The artist never prints.

notes.front: How do you recognise ukiyo-e visually?
notes.back: Flat unmodulated colour, bold black outlines, no cast shadows, asymmetric cropping, high or odd viewpoints, graded skies (bokashi), patterned textiles.

notes.front: Why is Islamic religious art largely non-figural?
notes.back: Hadith-based aversion to idolatry: mosques and Qur'ans avoid living beings, so creativity went into calligraphy, geometry and vegetal ornament. Figures do appear in secular manuscripts.

notes.text: Islamic ornament has three languages: {{c1::calligraphy}} (the Word made visible), {{c2::geometric pattern}} (star-and-polygon tessellations) and the {{c3::arabesque}} (endless scrolling vegetal forms).

notes.front: Why are Islamic geometric patterns infinite and repeating?
notes.back: A pattern with no centre or edge, built from a few compass constructions, evokes the unity and infinity of God and an order beyond the visible.
notes.analogy: A tiling algorithm: a small rule set generating an endless, perfectly consistent surface.

notes.front: What is a muqarnas?
notes.back: Honeycomb-like stacked niches beneath domes and in portals (Alhambra, Isfahan) that dissolve structure into pattern and light. A signature of Islamic architecture.

notes.front: How do you recognise a Persian or Mughal miniature?
notes.back: Small book illustration: brilliant flat colour, no cast shadows, high viewpoint with stacked tiers, fine line, patterned textiles and tiles, figures as types (Shahnameh, Akbarnama).

notes.front: Why does the Western 'progress toward realism' story mislead for other traditions?
notes.back: They never aimed at optical naturalism, so absence of perspective isn't 'primitive': they pursued line, pattern, spirit or ritual. Judge each tradition by its own goals.
